## Textbooks

### Open Educational Resources

Sufficient reading materials are provided via the course website — curated, remixed, or written to be perfectly in line with the teaching on the course. If you prefer physical textbooks, you are welcome to consult any Psychology research methods text (most cover the content we address), but I highly recommend the two books below (free online via the Goldsmiths Library).

### Recommended Texts (Available via Library)

Both textbooks are available as e-books through the VLE Reading List and the Goldsmiths Library (login required):

- **Coolican, H. (2017). *Research methods and statistics in psychology* (6th Ed.). Hodder and Stoughton.**
[Coolican *Research methods and statistics in psychology*](https://rl.talis.com/3/gold/items/8219BFAB-D96A-4F09-DCDA-3D08837C5F52.html?login=1)

- **Harris, P. (2008). *Designing and reporting experiments in psychology* (3rd Ed.). Open University Press.**
[Harris *Designing and reporting experiments in psychology*](https://rl.talis.com/3/gold/items/6C21CBA6-303B-DBC7-75D3-64F2AAF9F581.html?login=1)

::: {.callout-tip}
## Accessing E-Books
You'll need to log in with your Goldsmiths credentials. If you have trouble accessing, search via the [Reading List](https://learn.gold.ac.uk/mod/lti/view.php?id=1733027) or via the [library](https://librarysearch.gold.ac.uk/primo-explore/search?sortby=rank&vid=44GOL_VU1&lang=en_US).
:::

## Software

Software requirements are introduced gradually throughout the course. Whether you enjoy the technical side or prefer step-by-step guidance, the course materials have you covered.

### WebR (In-Browser)

All lab activities use **WebR**—R that runs directly in your browser. You don't need to install anything.

### R and RStudio (Optional)

If you want to install R on your own computer:

- [Download R](https://cran.r-project.org/)
- [Download RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)

## Online Statistics Resources

### Visual & Interactive

- [Seeing Theory](https://seeing-theory.brown.edu/) — Beautiful visual introduction to probability and statistics
- [Statistics by Jim](https://statisticsbyjim.com/) — Clear explanations of statistical concepts
- [Stat Trek](https://stattrek.com/) — Statistics tutorials and calculators

## R resources for Psychology undergraduates

- [Learning Statistics with R](https://learningstatisticswithr.com/) (Danielle Navarro)  
  Probably the most psych-undergrad-friendly open textbook: concepts first, then R, with the usual psych stats sequence (t-tests, ANOVA, regression, etc.).

- [R for Psychological Science](https://djnavarro.github.io/r4psych/) (Danielle Navarro)  
  More “learn R programming in a psych context” (great alongside a stats course).

- [PsyTeachR: Data Skills for Reproducible Research](https://psyteachr.github.io/) (PsyTeachR team)  
  A teachable, step-by-step route into tidyverse workflows and reproducible habits (projects, scripts, reporting), ideal for labs and dissertations.

## Hypothes.is Annotation

This module uses **Hypothes.is** for collaborative annotation. Think of it as a shared highlighter and sticky-note system that lives on top of web pages. You can highlight passages, add comments and questions, and see what other students have noticed or wondered about.

Why use it?

- **Active reading** - Annotation helps you engage with material rather than passively skimming
- **Shared learning** - See what confuses or interests your classmates (you're probably not alone!)
- **Ask questions in context** - Flag something unclear right where it appears, rather than trying to describe it later
- **Build a revision resource** - Your annotations become a personalised study guide

### Getting Started

1. **Create a free account** at [hypothes.is](https://hypothes.is/)
2. **Join our module group**: [Foundations26](https://hypothes.is/groups/qkwKVoRZ/foundations26)
3. **Install the browser extension** or use the bookmarklet (instructions on the Hypothes.is site)
4. **Start annotating** - Look for the sidebar on course pages, or activate the extension on any web page

::: {.callout-tip}
## Private vs Group Annotations
When you annotate, you can choose to make your notes **private** (only you see them), share them with our **Foundations26 group** (classmates see them), or make them **public** (the whole internet). For this module, group annotations are most useful - but private notes work well for personal revision.
:::
